newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel OKs Bristol-Myer's Excedrin for migraine.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel OKs Bristol-Myer's Excedrin for migraine.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Tuesday voted unanimously that Bristol-Myers Squibb's Excedrin Extra-Strength is effective for the temporary relief of migraine headache pain.
Migraine headaches affect 20-25 million Americans each year, three-quarters of them women.

A majority of the panel, 14 of the 17, felt it was safe as well. But the committee wanted to strengthen Excedrin E-S labeling to give guidance to consumers on how to differentiate among migraines and other headaches.
The FDA is not bound by its panels' advice, but usually follows it.
Excedrin E-S, sold since 1978, is the third-biggest pain reliever in the United States. BMS argued that since most migraineurs self-treat, an over-the-counter (OTC) drug is appropriate.
In a survey of migraineurs, BMS found that two-thirds of men and 57 percent of women use OTC's only.
"Self-treatment is the norm, not the exception," said Richard Lipton, a headache specialist with the Albert Einstein College of Medicine and a BMS representative.
Still, panelists worried that patients might not know what a migraine is, and said there could be side effects with chronic use of Excedrin E-S.
Each tablet contains 250 mg of acetaminophen, 250 mg of aspirin, and 65 mg of caffeine. BMS sought a dose of two tablets every six hours, to be taken for up to 10 days.
Large amounts of caffeine can trigger migraines, but small doses may help. BMS said it may also boost the analgesic's power.
Other triggers include light and temperature changes, diet, stress, depression, and hormonal fluctuation.
The condition is a huge economic burden, resulting in lost wages of $1.3 billion a year, said Jerry Miller of the Wellness Council .
Two prescription drugs are often used for severe migraines. Bristol-Myers' butorphanol (Stadol) has been popular since the nasal spray was launched in 1991, but has been pegged as addictive recently.
Glaxo Wellcome's sumitriptan (Imitrex) was launched in 1991. A self-injector came out in April, but the drug is expensive -- $12 a dose -- and has not penetrated the market.

Drugs in the same class are being tested by Zeneca Pharmaceuticals (zolmitriptan), Merck & Co. (rizatriptan), Glaxo Wellcome (naratriptan), and Pfizer (eletriptan). In early June, Merck said it hoped to soon seek FDA approval for rizatriptan (MAXALT).

BMS proved Excedrin E-S efficacy with three randomized, placebo-controlled trials, with 400 patients in each. Patients were recruited randomly through clinics. Those with severe migraines or who vomited more than 20% of the time were excluded.
Patients kept diaries and reported on pain and symptoms two hours after taking the medication -- either two tablets of Excedrin or placebo.

At two hours, 56-to-64% of Excedrin ES patients responded, compared to 31-to-37% on placebo. BMS also conducted a 900-person label comprehension study to see if consumers would understand new instructions about migraine.
When asked if they understood the need to see a doctor before taking Excedrin E-S if they have severe pain, vomiting, or needed bed rest with migraines, nine of ten did, said BMS.

From 1984 to 1997, BMS has received 2,400 reports of adverse events, but only 12 were serious, said Howard Hoffman of BMS. Most were either in the digestive tract, due to the aspirin, or in the nervous system, a result of the caffeine.
-- Washington newsroom, ((202-898-8300))
